R03-A-01: For much of the last century, the standard official response to an informal settlement was to remove it. Planners looked at a hillside of self-built houses, narrow lanes and improvised water connections and saw a problem of housing quality, to be solved by demolition and the construction of orderly blocks elsewhere, usually on cheaper land at the edge of the city. The logic seemed humane as well as tidy: people living without drains or secure walls would be given drains and secure walls. That the residents frequently resisted, and that many of the new blocks were half empty within a few years, was read as ingratitude, or as evidence that the poor did not know their own interests. A different reading is now more common, and it is more persuasive. An informal settlement is not simply a stock of poor dwellings; it is a working arrangement of livelihoods, and its location is usually its chief asset. A family that sells cooked food near a bus depot, a tailor who takes in work from a nearby market, a mother whose children attend a school within walking distance: all of them chose the site because of what it is close to. Relocation to a distant estate improves the walls while destroying the arrangement. The household may gain a toilet and lose two hours a day to travel, or lose the income that made the new rent payable at all. Seen this way, the empty blocks were not a puzzle but a verdict. Upgrading in place starts from this recognition. Instead of replacing the settlement, it adds what is missing: paved lanes, drainage, water and sewer lines, street lighting and, crucially, some form of secure tenure, so that residents can invest in their houses without fearing that the next official survey will mark them for demolition. Because the residents remain where they are, the networks that sustain them survive, and the public money spent goes into infrastructure rather than into reproducing, at great cost and in the wrong place, a community that already existed. None of this makes upgrading a universal remedy. Some settlements stand on land that floods every monsoon or slides in heavy rain, and to improve them in place is to invest in a future disaster. Nor is upgrading automatically benign: lanes widened for drainage can require the demolition of some houses, and a programme that installs pipes but withholds tenure leaves residents improved and still insecure. The case for upgrading is therefore not that informal settlements are good as they are, a romantic view their residents rarely share. It is that the people who built them understood something about the city that the planners who wished to clear them did not.
R03-A-02: Few words in urban debate do as much damage as 'density', largely because it is used, often by the same speaker within a single argument, to mean two quite different things. In its technical sense density is a ratio: the number of people, or of dwellings, on a given area of land. In ordinary speech it usually means something closer to crowding, the experience of too many people in too little room: a family of six in a single room, a queue that spills into the road, a train in which nobody can turn round. The two can occur together, but they need not, and treating them as one has shaped a century of planning. Consider two districts with the same number of residents per hectare. In the first, people live in tall apartment buildings with generous flats, set among parks and wide streets. In the second, the same population is packed into low houses, several households to a building, with lanes too narrow for a cart. On a map of density the districts are identical; to anyone who lives in them they could hardly be more different. Conversely, a scattered agricultural village, where extended families share a single dwelling, can be acutely crowded indoors while being nearly empty by the hectare. Density, in short, describes land; crowding describes the conditions of daily life. The confusion has a history. The diseases that ravaged industrial cities in the nineteenth century were widely blamed on density, and reformers responded by trying to spread people out. Yet what made those cities so lethal was a combination of overcrowded rooms, contaminated water and absent sewers, and where water and drains were improved, death rates in dense districts fell even though the districts often remained dense. The reformers were right that something was wrong; they were imprecise about what it was, and the imprecision outlived them, surviving in zoning codes and building regulations long after the sanitary conditions that had justified it had disappeared. This is not to say that density is costless. Many people living close together compete for parks, school places and quiet, and a district can feel oppressive even when no room in it is overcrowded. Perception counts, and planners who dismiss it will find their schemes resented. But the remedies differ. Crowding is relieved by more floor space per person and by services; the costs of density are managed by design, by open space and by the quality of the street. A policy that caps density in the name of relieving crowding may achieve neither, pushing people into fewer and more crowded rooms, or out to the edge of the city.
R03-A-03: In the last two decades the walkable neighbourhood has become one of the few planning ideals on which almost everyone claims to agree, and with agreement has come measurement. Composite indices now rate districts by the number of shops, schools and stops within a short radius, the density of street intersections and the share of homes near public transport. Estate agents quote such figures; municipal plans set targets for raising them. It would be churlish to deny the good these indices have done. They gave walking, long treated as what people did when they could not drive, a place in the arithmetic of planning, and they made visible how many districts had been designed as if nobody would ever arrive on foot. Yet what the indices measure is proximity, and proximity is not the same as walkability. A street can lie within five minutes of a pharmacy, a school and a bus stop and still be miserable to walk along: a narrow pavement beside four lanes of fast traffic, no shade under a summer sun, the blank walls of parking structures on either side, crossings that demand a long detour. Two districts with identical scores can therefore offer entirely different experiences, and the index has no way of registering the difference, because it counts what lies at the end of the walk and ignores the walk itself. This blindness is not accidental; it reflects an assumption that walking is chiefly a means of reaching places. For many people it is that, but it is also something more: the way a child learns a neighbourhood, the way an elderly resident keeps in contact with the world, the occasion for the chance encounters on which local life depends. These goods are produced en route, by the quality of the street, its pace, its frontages, its benches and its shade, not by the count of destinations. A measure built around destinations will systematically undervalue them. The danger is sharpest when the index ceases to be a description and becomes a target. A city told to raise its score can do so cheaply by permitting a few more shops near existing homes, while the hostile road that separates residents from those shops remains untouched. The number improves; the walk does not. None of this argues for abandoning measurement. It argues for remembering what the measurement leaves out, and for treating a high score as the beginning of an inquiry into a street rather than its conclusion.
R03-A-04: In many large cities, a good part of the open space created in recent decades does not belong to the public at all. Developers are permitted to build taller or larger than the rules would otherwise allow on condition that they provide a plaza, an arcade or a garden that anyone may enter. The arrangement looks like an elegant bargain: the city gains open space without paying for it, and the developer gains floor area worth far more than the ground surrendered. Critics have long complained that the resulting spaces are often bleak, hidden or quietly discouraging, with benches too narrow to sit on and guards who appear the moment anyone lingers. The usual form of the complaint is that these spaces are private, and that private space can never be truly public. This puts the matter in the wrong place. Ownership, by itself, settles very little. Many publicly owned squares are fenced at night, patrolled against skateboarders and stripped of seating to deter people who might sleep there, while some privately owned courtyards are generous, well kept and genuinely welcoming. If the test of publicness were the name on the title deed, we would have to call the first kind more public than the second, which is absurd. What makes a space public is better described as a set of permissions: the right to be there without a reason, to stay without buying anything, to gather with others, to hand out a leaflet or to hold a placard. These permissions are exactly what private management is tempted to withdraw, not out of malice but because each of them is a small risk to the owner and none of them earns anything. A plaza can be open to all in the formal sense while being governed by rules, often unpublished, that make it public only for the well dressed and the briefly passing. The question to ask is therefore not who owns a space but who writes its rules, and to whom the writers must answer. Seen this way, the bargain need not be abandoned; it needs to be completed. A city that trades floor area for open space is entitled to specify not only the dimensions of the plaza but the permissions that come with it, to publish them at the entrance, and to enforce them against owners as firmly as it enforces its building codes. Where it fails to do so, it has not acquired public space at all. It has paid, in floor area, for something that looks like a square and behaves like a lobby.
R03-A-05: Few settlement forms have been as consistently disparaged by writers as the suburb. For the better part of a century, novelists, critics and social scientists have described it in a nearly fixed vocabulary: monotonous rows of identical houses, lawns tended out of anxiety rather than pleasure, a life of commuting, shopping and television in which neighbours are near but never known. The suburb, in this account, is where individuality goes to be smoothed away. The striking thing about the indictment is not its severity but its uniformity, which ought to make us suspicious. A form of life chosen by many millions of households can hardly be as simple as the language used to dismiss it. Part of the indictment is sound. A district built around the car leaves those who cannot drive, the young, the old and the poor, stranded in a landscape in which nothing is within reach on foot. Zoning that separates homes from shops and workplaces by law multiplies journeys and empties the streets of the casual traffic through which neighbours become familiar. These are real costs, and they fall unevenly. But they are the costs of particular design decisions, and the critique of the suburb has rarely been content to remain at that level. Its deeper charge is cultural, and here it is weakest. It reads sameness of form as sameness of life, as if a street of similar houses must contain similar people living similar days; anyone who has knocked on the doors of such a street knows otherwise. It also tends to treat the wish for a garden, a quiet bedroom and a door one can close as a failure of imagination, when for families leaving cramped flats these were precisely the goods that city life had denied them. The critics, many of whom lived by choice in the centres of large cities, were often describing a preference they did not share as a pathology from which others suffered. None of this requires us to admire the suburb, or to ignore the costs of a pattern of building that consumes land and fuel at a great rate. It requires only that criticism be aimed at what can be changed. The desire for privacy and space is not a defect to be corrected; the absence of a shop within walking distance is. A suburb with a small centre, mixed uses and streets that a child can safely cross would answer most of the sound objections without asking anyone to want a different life.
R03-A-06: Arguments about gentrification tend to collapse into a single question: are the people who lived in a neighbourhood forced out when wealthier newcomers arrive? The question has the merit of being answerable, at least in principle. One can follow households over time, count how many leave, and compare the rate with that in neighbourhoods that have not changed. Suppose such a count found that long-standing residents of a gentrifying district left no faster than residents of similar districts elsewhere. Many would conclude that the harm of gentrification had been exaggerated, and that what remained of the complaint was mere nostalgia. That conclusion would be premature, because it assumes that the only way to lose a neighbourhood is to leave it. Consider the resident who stays. The grocer who extended credit has been replaced by a shop whose prices assume another income; the bench outside it, once a place to sit for an afternoon, now draws the attention of a security guard; the park is the same park, but the conduct expected in it has quietly changed, and complaints to the police now come from people she does not know, about behaviour that was ordinary a decade ago. She has not moved, and no count of departures will register her, yet the place in which she lives has been withdrawn from her as surely as if she had. To call this nostalgia is to mistake a loss of standing for a loss of scenery. The difficulty is that the language best suited to describing this loss, the language of a neighbourhood's 'character', is also the language most readily turned to the opposite purpose. Affluent districts invoke their character to resist new housing, to keep out flats that might bring poorer residents, to preserve a streetscape that functions, whatever its owners intend, as a barrier. If character means the look of the buildings and the tone of the streets, then the long-standing resident and the exclusionary homeowner are making the same argument, and it is not one that deserves much sympathy. The way out is to locate character not in the fabric of a place but in the relations it sustains: who is able to use it, on what terms, and with what claim to be heard. On this view, what the staying resident has lost is not a familiar shopfront but the practical standing she once had in her own street, and what the exclusionary homeowner defends is not a set of relations at all but the absence of people who might form new ones. The distinction will not settle every case, and it asks more of planners than a count of departures does. But it allows us to take the quieter harms of gentrification seriously without lending our sympathy to every resident who would prefer that nothing near them ever changed.
R03-A-07: The familiar story of urbanisation runs in one direction. People leave the countryside for the city, struggle for a generation in its least desirable quarters, and are eventually absorbed, their children speaking the city's idiom and regarding the village as a place of grandparents and holidays. Migration, on this account, is a passage with a beginning and an end, and the only question worth asking about a migrant is how far along it he has come. The story is not false; it describes what happened to many families in many countries. But it has acquired the status of a norm, against which other patterns are measured and found wanting, and this has made it difficult to see a pattern that is, in much of the world, at least as common. A large number of those who work in cities never complete the journey the story describes. They come for a season of construction or a few years in a factory, return for the harvest, a wedding or an illness in the family, and come back again, sometimes to the same city and sometimes to another. Their earnings pay school fees and debts in the village; the village holds their land, their elders and, often, their spouses and children. A household can live this way for decades, and many do. Seen through the one-way story, such people are migrants who have not yet settled, a transitional population whose double life is a symptom of incomplete integration. Seen on its own terms, the pattern looks rather different: a way of spreading risk across two places, so that a lost job in the city or a failed crop in the village need not be ruinous, because the other place remains. The distinction matters because city governments have tended to act on the first reading. A resident whose household is registered elsewhere, whose stay is irregular, and whose address is a worksite or a shared rented room is easily treated as a visitor: excluded from subsidised housing, from schools for the children who come along, from the electoral roll, and from the attention of politicians who answer to those who are on it. The exclusion then produces the very evidence that justifies it. Denied a secure foothold in the city, the circular migrant has every reason to keep the village in reserve, and the persistence of his village ties is then cited as proof that he never really belonged. It would be a mistake to romanticise circulation in its turn. Some who move back and forth would settle in the city if they could, and return to the village only because the city offers them nothing to stay for; for them, circularity is less a strategy than a sentence. Others genuinely prefer a life lived in two places and would keep it even if the city were more welcoming. The difficulty is that from the outside the two groups look identical, and a policy designed for one will misjudge the other. What follows is not a single programme but a change in the condition attached to belonging. A city that made its entitlements portable, that allowed a worker to enrol his children in school without proving permanent residence, and that encouraged cheap rental housing suited to stays of months rather than decades would serve both groups at once. It would allow those who wish to settle to do so, and those who wish to circulate to circulate without penalty. What it would cease to do is demand that a person surrender one home as the price of being recognised in another.
R03-A-08: In the language of property, home and ownership have become almost interchangeable. To own the place one lives in is to 'have a home'; to rent is to be on the way to one, or to have failed to arrive. The equation is so familiar that it seems less a claim than a definition, and policies built on it, from subsidised mortgages to the sale of public housing to its tenants, present themselves not as choices among ways of housing people but as the extension of home itself to those who lack it. Yet if one asks what people mean when they say that a place feels like home, the answers rarely mention title. They mention routines that have settled into the rooms, objects arranged by one's own hand, the confidence that one will be there next year, the freedom to decide who comes in, the ability to paint a wall or plant a window box or keep a dog. Home, in this sense, is less a thing one possesses than something one does, a practice of shaping a space and being shaped by it over time. And a practice of this kind needs two conditions: enough control over the space to shape it, and enough security of tenure to make the shaping worthwhile. Neither condition is the same as ownership, though ownership has usually supplied both. A tenant on a twelve-month lease who may be asked to leave at short notice, who must seek permission to hang a picture, and whose rent can rise without limit, has good reason not to invest himself in his rooms; he is camping, however long he stays. But the cause of his condition is not that he rents. It is that his tenancy is short, revocable and hedged with prohibitions. Where tenancies are long, rents predictable and tenants free to alter their surroundings within reason, renters make homes much as owners do, while an owner whose mortgage payments consume most of his income, and who fears that a lost job means a lost house, may know the very precariousness that the equation reserves for tenants. None of this means that ownership confers nothing distinctive. The owner can knock down a wall, not merely paint it; he can leave the house to his children; he answers to no landlord. A tenant, however secure, lives in a space whose final shape is decided by someone else. These are real goods, and it would be odd to deny that many people want them for good reasons. The objection is not to ownership but to the assumption that it is the only door into home, an assumption that directs public effort towards turning tenants into owners while leaving the conditions of tenancy, under which a large and often growing share of urban households live, largely untouched. The cost of that assumption is not only sentimental. A household that expects to move at a landlord's word does not join the school committee, does not plant a tree it will not see grow, does not learn the names of neighbours it may lose within the year. Schools, associations and local shops all depend on residents who expect to stay long enough for their efforts to bear fruit. The practices through which people make a home are continuous with those through which they make a neighbourhood, so that insecurity inside the door becomes thinness of attachment outside it. To treat home as a matter of title is therefore to misunderstand not only what renters lack but what cities lose when they lack it.
